canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Direct polynomial tangent
canonicalQuestion.questionText: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=3x^2-2x+1$ at $x=-1$.
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=6x-2$, so $m=-8$ and the point is $(-1,6)$. Hence $y-6=-8(x+1)$, giving $y=-8x-2$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Evaluate the derivative and the curve separately at $x=-1$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Substituting $x=-1$ into the curve but not into the derivative.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Direct polynomial tangent
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-1$, so $m=-1$ and the point is $(0,5)$. Thus $y=-x+5$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Keep the constant term in the curve, but not in its derivative.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Dropping the negative sign in the gradient.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Direct polynomial tangent
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=4x^3+2x-3$, so $m=3$ and the point is $(1,1)$. Therefore $y-1=3(x-1)$, giving $y=3x-2$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Differentiate every non-constant term before evaluating at $x=1$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Setting the derivative equal to zero as if finding a stationary point.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Negative leading coefficient
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-3x^2+6x$, so $m=3$ and the point is $(1,4)$. Hence $y-4=3(x-1)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Retain the negative sign when differentiating the cubic term.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Differentiating $-x^3$ as $3x^2$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Fractional intercept
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x^3-3$, so $m=-5$. Using $(-1,\frac72)$ gives $y-\frac72=-5(x+1)$, hence $y=-5x-\frac32$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: The contact point is $(-1,\frac72)$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Making a sign error when expanding $-5(x+1)$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Supplied contact point
canonicalQuestion.questionText: The point $(2,18)$ lies on $y=2x^3+x^2-3x+4$. Determine the tangent there.
canonicalQuestion.hint: The point is already supplied; calculate only the gradient.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Recalculating the supplied point incorrectly.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Negative contact value
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=4x^3-8x$, so $m=4$ and the point is $(-1,-2)$. Thus $y+2=4(x+1)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Substitute $-1$ carefully into both expressions.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Treating $(-1)^3$ as positive.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Descending quadratic
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-2-2x$, so $m=2$ and the point is $(-2,4)$. Hence $y-4=2(x+2)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Keep both negative signs in the derivative.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Using the contact value $-2$ as the gradient.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Zero curve value
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=9x^2+4x$, so $m=13$ and the point is $(1,0)$. Therefore $y=13(x-1)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: The contact point lies on the $x$-axis.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Writing $y=13x$ and ignoring the contact point.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Quartic with negative gradient
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-8x^3+2x$, so $m=-6$ and the point is $(1,5)$. Thus $y-5=-6(x-1)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Find the gradient and contact value independently.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Losing the negative sign while rearranging.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Negative contact value
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+12x$, so $m=-12$ and the point is $(-2,19)$. Hence $y-19=-12(x+2)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: In point-gradient form, $x-(-2)=x+2$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Writing $x-2$ instead of $x+2$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Multi-term quartic
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=8x^3-10x+1$, so $m=3$ and the point is $(-1,-4)$. Therefore $y+4=3(x+1)$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Differentiate every term before substituting.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Omitting the derivative of the linear term.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Simplify before differentiating
canonicalQuestion.questionText: For $x\ne0$, find the tangent to $y=\frac{x^3+2x^2-3x}{x}$ at $x=2$.
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $y=x^2+2x-3$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x+2$. At $x=2$, $m=6$ and the point is $(2,5)$, giving $y=6x-7$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Simplify the curve before differentiating.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Applying the power rule to the unsimplified quotient term by term.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Fractional contact coordinate
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-2x$. At $x=\frac12$, the gradient is $m=\frac12$ and the curve value is $1$. Hence $y-1=\frac12(x-\frac12)$, or $4y=2x+3$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Keep the contact coordinate and gradient as exact fractions.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Treating $\left(\frac12\right)^2$ as $\frac12$ when evaluating the derivative.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Direct polynomial with negative gradient
canonicalQuestion.hint: Substitute $x=-1$ separately into the curve and its derivative.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Treating the even power $(-1)^2$ as negative in the derivative.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Fractional coefficient and intercept
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2-4x+5$, so $m=1$ at $x=2$. The curve value is $\frac{11}{3}$, hence $y-\frac{11}{3}=x-2$, or $3y=3x+5$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Keep the curve value exact before forming the line equation.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Differentiating $\frac13x^3$ as $\frac13x^2$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Fractional gradient
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac12x^2+2x-2$. At $x=-1$, $m=-\frac72$ and the curve value is $\frac{17}{6}$. Thus $y-\frac{17}{6}=-\frac72(x+1)$, which rearranges to $21x+6y+4=0$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Keep both the gradient and contact value as exact fractions.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Using the negative reciprocal of $-\frac72$ instead of the tangent gradient itself.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Multi-term odd-power polynomial
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-3+6x^2-5x^4$, so $m=-2$ at $x=-1$. The point is $(-1,7)$, giving $y-7=-2(x+1)$ and $y=-2x+5$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Evaluate each odd power carefully at $x=-1$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Assigning a negative value to the even powers in the derivative.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Linear-inside composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=3(x-2)^2$, so $m=3$ and the point is $(3,2)$. Hence $y=3x-7$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Use the original curve to find the point.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Forgetting the final $+1$ in the curve value.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Scaled linear-inside composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=6(3x+2)-5$. At $x=0$, $m=7$ and the point is $(0,4)$. Thus $y-4=7x$, giving $y=7x+4$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Differentiate both the composite term and the separate linear term.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Differentiating the bracket correctly but omitting the derivative of $-5x$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Decreasing composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-4(3-x)^3$, so $m=-4$ and the point is $(2,1)$. Hence $y=-4x+9$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: The derivative of $3-x$ is $-1$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Missing the negative inside derivative.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: High-degree direct polynomial
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=10x^4-15x^2+8x$. At $x=-1$, $m=-13$ and the curve value is $0$. Therefore $y=-13(x+1)$, or $y=-13x-13$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Evaluate the curve and its derivative independently at the negative coordinate.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Making the odd-power terms positive when substituting $x=-1$ into the curve.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Cubic composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=3(2x^2-x)^2(4x-1)$, so $m=9$ and the point is $(1,1)$. Thus $y=9x-8$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: The inside derivative is $4x-1$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Using the inside value $1$ as the gradient.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Quadratic-inside composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=2(x^2-3x+4)(2x-3)$, so $m=-4$ and the point is $(1,4)$. Hence $y=-4x+8$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Evaluate both factors of the derivative.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Substituting into only one factor of the derivative.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Supplied point with fractional gradient
canonicalQuestion.questionText: The point $\left(3,\frac{23}{2}\right)$ lies on $y=\frac12x^3-2x+4$. Determine the tangent there.
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac32x^2-2$, so at $x=3$ the gradient is $\frac{23}{2}$. Using the supplied point gives $y-\frac{23}{2}=\frac{23}{2}(x-3)$, or $2y=23x-46$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: The contact point is supplied, so only the gradient needs to be calculated from the curve.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Using the supplied $y$-coordinate as the gradient because both values happen to be $\frac{23}{2}$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Negative-power composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-2(x+1)^{-3}$, so $m=-\frac14$ and the point is $(1,\frac14)$. Hence $x+4y=2$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Keep the gradient and point values exact.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Reducing the power incorrectly.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Reciprocal quadratic composite
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-(2x+2)(x^2+2x+2)^{-2}$, so $m=-\frac12$ and the point is $(0,\frac12)$. Thus $x+2y=1$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Differentiate the reciprocal form with the chain rule.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Forgetting the squared denominator after differentiating.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Calculator polynomial tangent
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=4.8x^2-4.8x+0.7$. At $x=1.5$, the gradient is $4.3$ and the curve value is $2.25$. Hence $y-2.25=4.3(x-1.5)$, so $y=4.3x-4.2$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Use the calculator to evaluate the curve and derivative values accurately before forming the line.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Rounding the contact value or gradient before completing the line equation.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Composite at a negative x-value
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=6x(x^2+2)^2$, so $m=-54$ and the point is $(-1,27)$. Hence $y=-54x-27$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Take care with the factor $2x$ at $x=-1$.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Losing the negative sign from $2x$.

canonicalQuestion.subject: Higher Maths
canonicalQuestion.title: Negative inside value
canonicalQuestion.workedSolution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-16x(1-2x^2)^3$, so $m=16$ and the point is $(1,1)$. Thus $y=16x-15$.
canonicalQuestion.hint: Preserve the sign of the cubed inside value.
canonicalQuestion.commonMistake: Assuming the gradient is negative from the derivative's first factor alone.
